original_value: Mobile sensors have already proven to be helpful in different aspects of people’s everyday lives such as fitness, gaming, navigation, etc. However, illegitimate access to these sensors results in a malicious program running with an exploit path. While the users are benefiting from richer and more personalized apps, the growing number of sensors introduces new security and privacy risks to end users and makes the task of sensor management more complex. In this paper, first, we discuss the issues around the security and privacy of mobile sensors. We investigate the available sensors on mainstream mobile devices and study the permission policies that Android, iOS and mobile web browsers offer for them. Second, we reflect the results of two workshops that we organized on mobile sensor security. In these workshops, the participants were introduced to mobile sensors by working with sensor-enabled apps. We evaluated the risk levels perceived by the participants for these sensors after they understood the functionalities of these sensors. The results showed that knowing sensors by working with sensor-enabled apps would not immediately improve the users’ security inference of the actual risks of these sensors. However, other factors such as the prior general knowledge about these sensors and their risks had a strong impact on the users’ perception. We also taught the participants about the ways that they could audit their apps and their permissions. Our findings showed that when mobile users were provided with reasonable choices and intuitive teaching, they could easily self-direct themselves to improve their security and privacy. Finally, we provide recommendations for educators, app developers, and mobile users to contribute toward awareness and education on this topic.

result.paraphrase: Mobile sensors are already useful in many everyday activities, including fitness, gaming, and navigation. Yet unauthorized access to these sensors can enable malicious programs to exploit them. As users gain richer, more personalized apps, the growing number of sensors also brings new security and privacy risks and makes sensor management more complicated. In this paper, we first examine the security and privacy concerns surrounding mobile sensors. We review the sensors available on mainstream mobile devices and analyze the permission policies provided for them by Android, iOS, and mobile web browsers. Next, we summarize findings from two workshops we organized on mobile sensor security. In these workshops, participants learned about mobile sensors by using sensor-enabled apps. After understanding what these sensors do, we measured how risky the participants believed they were. The results showed that learning about sensors through sensor-enabled apps did not immediately improve users’ judgment of the real risks. However, other influences, such as prior general knowledge about the sensors and their risks, had a strong effect on perception. We also instructed participants on how to audit their apps and permissions. Our findings indicate that when mobile users are given sensible options and intuitive instruction, they can readily guide themselves toward better security and privacy. Finally, we offer recommendations for educators, app developers, and mobile users to help raise awareness and support education on this topic.
